paper_metadata.title: Time-dependent subcritical crack growth and its mechanism in Ni-based single crystal superalloys at 500 °C

evidence.quote: Time-dependent subcritical crack growth and its mechanism in Ni-based single crystal superalloys at 500 °C

The subcritical crack growth behavior under sustained loading and its microscopic mechanism in < 100 > oriented single crystal (SC) Ni-based superalloys subjected to a relatively low temperature condition (500 ◦ C) are critically investigated.

The magnified image in Fig. 5 (a) reveals two distinct types of dislocation contrast in the γ ′ phase: one parallel to the < 100 > direction and another one to the < 110 > direction, both of which have fairly rectilinear morphology.

The character of discrete dislocations is observed at a position slightly away from the crack tip as shown in the lower micrograph. Again, two types of dislocation contrast parallel to either < 100 > or < 110 > direction can be clearly seen in the γ ′ phase.

Note that the distribution of oxygen along the crack wake is not uniform: spike like intrusions are formed at the position of the γ phase, see the arrow heads in Fig. 8 (b). This indicates that the oxidation formation is more localized in the γ’ phase.
The TDCG rate (d a /d t ) of both alloys were found to be significantly small (not more than the order of 10 − 10 m/s) and weakly dependent on the crack length, i.e. the K value.

The TDCG rate of alloy B, on the other hand, initially increases to the order of 10 − 10 m/s and subsequently shifts to a gradual increase with similar ups/downs, but it still does not exceed 10 − 9 m/s during most of the life.

These points strongly suggest that the dislocation-mediated micro-oxidation process plays a major role in the observed anisotropic TDCG mechanism that eventually leads to the anomalous d a /d t - K property.

The plateau behavior in the d a /d t - K diagram (so-called stage II regime) of SCC has been correlated to the emergence of crack branching, see e.g. refs [ 30 – 32 ]. From a mechanical viewpoint, such a phenomenon has been explained by focusing on the local K property of a bifurcated crack [ 28 ]. After losing K value by a branching event, each branched crack gradually grows again and restore its own local (microscopic) K value until it is lost again by the next branching. When such a discrete crack growth is viewed macroscopically, average growth rate appears to stay rather constant despite the total crack length monotonically increases.
